Abstract
The 
antidiabetic 
activity 
and 
potential 
underlying 
mechanism 
of 
a 
polysaccharide-protein complex (PSP) from Corbicula fluminea was determined in 
streptozotoxin (STZ)-induced diabetic rats. PSP exhibited inhibitory activity (in vitro) against 
α-glucosidase and α-amylase via reversible competitive inhibition pattern with a stronger 
inhibition on α-glucosidase. Dietary administration of PSP had potent antidiabetic activities 
in vivo, which was evidenced by that PSP alleviated body weight loss and organ injures, 
reduced fasting blood glucose, elevated glucose tolerance, and ameliorated lipid metabolism 
and hepatic functions, as well as attenuated oxidative stress in STZ-treated diabetic rats. 
Furthermore, our results demonstrated that the antidiabetic activities of PSP were associated 
with activation of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B signaling pathway in 
STZ-treated rats. These findings supported the potential of PSP to be used as a functional 
ingredient for functional and medical foods to inhibit diabetes mellitus and its complications.
Keywords: Corbicula fluminea; Polysaccharide–protein complex; Antidiabetic activity; 
Signaling pathway

1. Introduction
There has been a sharp increase in the incidence of diabetes mellitus (DM) globally in 
recent years. DM is becoming a serious public health problem all over the world. In China, 
the number of diabetes patients is now the second highest in the world (after the United States) 
and increasing at an alarming rate.1 Although traditional hypoglycemic drugs, including 
insulin, biguanides, and sulfonylureas, can temporarily reduce blood glucose level, they are 
often associated with many serious side effects, such as hypoglycemia, large blood glucose 
fluctuations, and gastrointestinal reactions, which have high cost, thereby greatly limiting 
their application in clinical practice.2 Therefore, the development of new, safe, and efficient 
hypoglycemic drugs or functional foods from natural sources to prevent and treat diabetes 
and its complications is of great significance.
Over the last decade, numerous studies have demonstrated that polysaccharides (PSs) 
derived from natural resources exerted prominent antidiabetic effects with few or no side 
effects through mainly preventing oxidative stress damage and/or increasing insulin 
sensitivity, and could be developed as new complementary or alternative hypoglycemic drugs 
to treat and/or prevent the occurrence of DM in clinic.2-4 Corbicula fluminea, also called 
Asian clam, is a freshwater bivalve mollusk widely distributed in East Asian countries, such 
as Japan, Korea, and China. It has high edible value and health function. C. fluminea as the 
traditional Chinese medicine has exhibited multiple functions, such as appetizing, purging 
milk, brightening eyes, dieresis, removing dampness and toxin, treating liver disease and 
measles, reducing fever, relieving cough and phlegm, and relieving wine effects.5 Modern 
pharmacological studies have demonstrated that PSs are among the major active components

of C. fluminea with diverse biological activities, including antitumor and antioxidant 
activities.6,7 In our research, a novel and water-soluble polysaccharide-protein complex (PSP) 
was separated from C. fluminea by applying the enzyme-assisted three-phase partitioning 
(TPP) technique, and the resultant PSP showed prominent free radical scavenging ability and 
antioxidant capacity in vitro.8 Meanwhile, many researchers have revealed that symptoms of 
hyperglycemia are closely related to the generation of excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) 
and associated oxidative stress, especially in the liver, kidneys, and pancreas.9 
Supplementation with antioxidants is an effective alternative for attenuating hyperglycemia 
symptoms, thereby leading to the prevention and treatment of DM and its complications. 
Based on the abovementioned findings, it was hypothesized that the antioxidative PSP could 
be explored as a potential hypoglycemic agent for the prevention and treatment of DM and its 
complications. However, studies on the antidiabetic activity of the PSP and its corresponding 
possible mechanism are lacking or few.
The objective of this study was to determine the hypoglycemic effects of the PSP both in 
vitro against α-amylase and α-glucosidase activities and in vivo against streptozotocin 
(STZ)-induced diabetes in rats. The potential antidiabetic mechanisms of the PSP were also 
investigated in this study.

superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), catalase (CAT), 
malondialdehyde (MDA), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) 
were purchased from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, China). 
Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K), protein kinase B (Akt), phospho-Akt (p-Akt), glycogen

were purchased from Beijing CWBIO (CWBIO, Beijing, China). All other chemicals and 
solvents were of laboratory grade and used without further purification.

The in vitro hypoglycemic effect of the PSP was investigated through α-amylase and 
α-glucosidase inhibitory activity assays.10 The PSP was previously dissolved in distilled

2.3. Animals and experimental design
Forty male SD rats (150 ± 30 g, five weeks old) were obtained from the Experimental 
Animal Center of Jiangsu University (Zhenjiang, China). Before the experiment, all rats were 
housed in sanitized polypropylene cages under the standard conditions (12 h light/12 h dark 
cycle; ambient temperature: 23± 0.5 °C; humidity: 50± 5%) with free access to commercial 
standard chow and tap water. After 7 days of acclimatization, eight rats were randomly 
selected and assigned to the normal control (NC) group and given 6 mL/kg body weight (BW) 
physiological saline solution (PSS, 0.9%, w/v) by intragastric administration daily for the 
entire experiment period. The other rats were then fasted for 12 h and injected 
intraperitoneally with freshly prepared STZ solution in 0.1 M citrate buffer (pH 4.5) at a dose 
of 65 mg/kg BW. After 3 days, the fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels of rats were greater 
than 11.1 mmol/L and less than 33.3 mmol/L, thereby indicating the successful establishment 
of STZ-induced diabetic rat models, which were used for subsequent experiments. These 
STZ-induced diabetic rats were randomly divided into four groups. One group was regarded

During the experiment period, FBG levels of all the rats after fasting 12 h were weekly 
measured by a One-touch Glucometer with test strips (Johnson & Johnson) from the tail vein. 
At the last 7 days of treatment, the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was also performed, as 
described in a previous study.11 All rats were administered intragastrically with 2.0 g/kg BW 
glucose after fasting overnight. Then, blood samples were collected from the tail vein at 
intervals of 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min. The FBG levels were immediately measured by the 
glucometer. The glucose tolerance was expressed as the area under the blood glucose curve 
[AUC, mmol/(L·h)], which was equal to (1/4 FBG at 0 h + 1/2 FBG at 0.5 h + 3/4 FBG at 1.0 
h + 1/2 FBG at 2.0 h).
After 28 days of treatment, all the rats were fasted overnight, weighed, and anesthetized 
with 10% chloral hydrate intraperitoneally. Blood samples were then collected and 
centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The obtained serum was stored at -80 °C before 
further measurement. After the rats were euthanized, the liver, kidney, spleen, and thymus 
were excised immediately, and then weighed after washing with ice-cold PSS to calculate the 
organ index, i.e., each organ’s weight as a percentage of BW. Two small pieces of liver 
section from the same rat were fixed with 10% paraformaldehyde for histopathological

2.4. Biochemical analysis
The ALT, AST, SOD, CAT, and GSH-Px activities and the serum contents of MDA, TG,

supplied by Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, China).

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect of PSP on α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activities

enzymes, such as α-glucosidase and α-amylase, is a simple and effective strategy for DM 
treatment and/or prevention.3,12 The α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activity assays 
are widely used to determine the in vitro hypoglycemic effects of bioactive compounds from 
natural sources.12,13 Moreover, numerous studies have also proved that PSs showed excellent 
α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activities.2,4,10 In the current work, the hypoglycemic 
potential (in vitro) of the PSP obtained from C. fluminea was investigated by α-amylase and 
α-glucosidase inhibitory activtiy assays (Fig. 1A and 1B). The inhibitory activities of the PSP 
against α-glucosidase and α-amylase significantly and dose-dependently increased with 
increasing concentration of PSP from 0.5 to 5.0 mg/mL. Under the treatment of 5.0 mg/mL 
PSP, the α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activities of the PSP were 84.55 ± 1.04 % 
and 58.27 ± 5.46 %, respectively, which were significantly lower than those obtained from 
acarbose (92.78 ± 0.19% and 70.87 ± 2.76%). This result suggested that the PSP had 
potential α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activities. Moreover, the inhibitory ability 
of PSP on α-glucosidase was stronger than that on α-amylase within the range of measured 
concentrations, as shown in a previous study.14 This finding may be attributed to the 
differences in the mechanism of action between α-glucosidase and α-amylase.
To further verify the inhibition pattern of PSP, the inhibition kinetics of PSP against 
α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activities were evaluated by Lineweaver-Burk plots; 
and the obtained results are illustrated in Figs. 1C-F. As shown in Fig. 1C, it could be clearly 
found that the linear double reciprocal plots intersected the y-axis and the intercept remained 
unchanged, whereas the slope increased with increasing substrate concentration. That is to 
say, the maximum reaction rate (Vmax) did not change, but the M-K constant (Km) increased

Similarly, Shan et al. (2016) pointed out that fucoidan from Fucus vesiculosus (FvF) 
exhibited prominent α-glucosidase inhibitory activity, with an IC50 value of 67.9 μg/mL.15 
The confirmed competitive inhibitory pattern of the FvF was similar to that of known 
α-glucosidase inhibitors, such as acarbose.16 Meanwhile, the results obtained from Figs. 1D 
and 1F also indicated that the PSP is a competitive inhibitor with respect to α-amylase for 
starch in a reversible fashion. In the same way Xu et al. (2018) reported that an acidic 
heteropolysaccharide (BCP-2) from blackcurrant fruits exhibited moderate α-amylase 
inhibitory activity (37.39%) and strong α-glucosidase inhibitory activity (78.42%), and the 
inhibitory effect of BCP-2 on α-amylase was reversible and showed a competitively 
inhibitory process,17 which was similar with our findings. By contrast, Kasipandi et al. (2019) 
investigated the influences of in vitro gastrointestinal digestion on the α-glucosidase and 
α-amylase inhibiting properties of water-soluble polysaccharides from Opilia amentacea roxb 
fruit (OAFP), and revealed that pre and post-digested OAFP effectively inhibited 
α-glucosidase and α-amylase by non-competitive inhibition modes,18 which was different 
from our data. Based on the abovementioned findings, we suggested that the PSP could be 
developed as a good α-glucosidase inhibitor to retard postprandial hyperglycemia in diabetes 
patients. It was then further subjected to the subsequent in vivo antidiabetic activity through a

3.2. Effect of PSP on BW gain and organ indexes in STZ-induced diabetic rats
In the current work, the STZ-induced diabetic rat model was applied to evaluate the 
antidiabetic activity of PSP in vivo. Table 1 showed the effect of the PSP on BW gain and 
organ indexes of the STZ-induced diabetic rats. After 4 weeks of feeding, the BW gain in the 
normal group was significantly higher than those in STZ-induced diabetic groups (MC, PC, 
PSP-L, PSP-H). This may be due to the fact that STZ led to BW loss or the degradation of 
structural proteins in rats with diabetes. However, the BW gains in the PSP-L, PSP-H and PC 
groups were siginificantly higher than that in STZ-induced diabetic rats in the MC group 
(P<0.05), which indicated that the PSP treatments could significantly and dose-dependently 
alleviate the BW loss in STZ-induced diabetic rats. Meanwhile, as shown in Fig. 2A, the NC 
group showed a higher weight gain tendency than STZ-induced diabetic groups. Continuous 
treatments with metformin and PSP at different doses led to increasing tendency of BW 
compared with the MC group during the 4 weeks of experiment. Wang et al. (2014) reported 
that the weight loss was positively related to the abnormalities in glucose intolerance, which 
was attributed to insulin resistence/inadequate secretion or hyperlipidemia in DM.19 Thus, the 
intervention of PSP for 4 weeks could ameliorate the weight loss of STZ-induced diabetic 
rats. Similar results were also observed in previous studies.20, 21

were observed, except for the spleen of STZ-induced diabetic rats. However, after 4 weeks of

3.3. Effect of PSP on FBG levels and OGTT in STZ-induced diabetic rats
In the present study, the FBG levels of normal and STZ-induced diabetic rats were 
measured weekly, and the results are presented in Fig. 2B. During the experiment, the FBG 
levels of rats in the NC group were stable and significantly lower than those of the other four 
STZ-induced diabetic groups. At the beginning of the test (0 week), the STZ-induced diabetic 
groups exhibited strikingly increased FBG levels compared with the NC group (P<0.01), and 
their FBG levels were all higher than 20 mmol/L, thereby suggesting the successful 
establishment of the STZ-induced diabetic rat model. After 1 week of treatment, the FBG 
level of the PC group treated with metformin (75 mg/kg BW) showed a significant decrease 
compared with the MC group (P<0.01). However, oral administrations with PSP cannot 
reduce the FBG levels of STZ-induced diabetic groups in the first 2 weeks, and no 
statistically significant differences were observed. After 3 weeks of continuous 
administrations with PSP, the FBG levels in PSP-L and PSP-H groups decreased significantly

4. Conclusions
In summary, PSP obtained from C. fluminea not only exhibited potential α-glucosidase 
and α-amylase inhibitory activities in vitro, but also exerted antidiabetic benefits in 
STZ-induced diabetic rats in vivo by alleviating weight loss and organ injures, reducing FBG 
levels, elevating glucose tolerance, ameliorating lipid metabolism and hepatic function, and 
attenuating oxidative stress. RT-PCR and Western blot analyses revealed that PSP had a 
positive effect on antidiabetic activity by activating the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in 
STZ-induced diabetic rats. Therefore, the present findings suggested that PSP might be a 
promising functional food ingredient or dietary supplement for potentially applications in the 
treatment and prevention of DM and its complications.
